title: Into Battle
summary: The vajra and the lotus go to war: an army musters, the towns of objects and senses are destroyed, drum and conch proclaim the unstruck melodies, the forces of existence and delusion are driven off, fire burns away the faults of the three maṇḍalas, and the refrain names the king, emptiness, great bliss; at the end Kukkurīpāda raises his finger and declares that this conquers the three worlds by great bliss. The Bengali is lost, and the song is translated here from its Tibetan translation. Munidatta, whose comment also survives mostly in Tibetan, reads the vajra and the lotus as means and wisdom and says the towns fall at the mere hearing of the name ‘great bliss’; his one surviving Sanskrit passage takes the three worlds as the fault of appearance of body, speech and mind, conquered by great bliss.

lines.translit: /pa Da ha zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs kuk+ku rI pa'i zhabs kyi'o/
lines.gloss: Paḍaha (name) · so-called · melody · of Kukkurīpa · feet (honorific, -pāda) · of (it is)

flags.note: The heading names the melody only as pa Da ha. I file it under Paṭamañjarī as a shortened form, as the glossary does: in other headings the Tibetan translation gives that rāga as pa Ta ha many+dza ri or pa Da ha many+dza ri, or half-translates it (pa Ta ha'i snye ma, pa Da ha'i tshogs pa, rnga'i tshogs pa, ‘cluster of drums’), so pa Da ha looks like the name with -mañjarī dropped. A rāga called Paṭaha, or the drum paṭaha itself (pa Ta ha in song 19), cannot be ruled out; a drum-named melody would suit a battle song, but that is only a guess. Alternative: ‘Rāga Paḍaha’ (or ‘Paṭaha’) kept in source form.
The heading survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293); it names the poet kuk+ku rI pa'i zhabs, ‘Kukkurīpāda’.

lines.translit: /rdo rje chu skyes g.yul ngor zhugs/
lines.gloss: vajra · water-born (lotus) · to the battlefront · entered

flags.note: zhugs is the past form of 'jug, ‘enter’, and also its imperative. I take it as past, ‘went into’, in line with the other narrative verbs (bcom, byas, bsdus); ‘Vajra and lotus, go into battle!’ is grammatically possible.
g.yul ngo is literally ‘the face of battle’, the battlefront; ‘went into battle’ keeps the sense. chu skyes, ‘water-born’, is an ordinary Tibetan word for the lotus.

lines.translit: /mnyam nyid sbyor ba'i dmag dpung tshogs/

flags.note: I read mnyam nyid sbyor ba'i dmag dpung as ‘the army of union in sameness’ and tshogs as the verb ‘mustered, gathered’. Alternatives: ‘the army joined (yoked) in sameness’; or tshogs as a noun, ‘the host of the army of union in sameness’, in apposition to 1a. sbyor ba can also mean yoga or application. Munidatta's Tibetan paraphrase speaks of joining in sameness (mnyam pa nyid du sbyor ba, cp.48.m3).
‘union’ is linked to the glossary's mela, whose Tibetan forms include sbyor ba; the entry was made for Old Bengali melā in song 27. Confirm, or leave sbyor ba unlinked.

lines.translit: /yul dang dbang po'i grong rnams bcom/
lines.gloss: object (also ‘land’) · and · of sense faculty (also ‘lord’) · towns · destroyed

flags.note: yul is the glossary's visaya, ‘sense objects’, but the town entry bars ‘sense objects’ inside any verse line where the town is, so the line has ‘objects’ (linked to visaya). See questions.

yul also means ‘land, country’ and dbang po ‘lord, ruler’: ‘the towns of the land and its lords’ would also suit the battle. I follow the technical sense, sense objects and sense faculties, which the glossary gives and Munidatta's comment confirms (cp.48.m4).
bcom is the past of 'joms, ‘destroy, conquer’. No agent is named; ‘were destroyed’ leaves it open.

lines.translit: /stong nyid rgyal po bde chen ming /

flags.note: stong nyid rgyal po: apposition, ‘emptiness, the king’ (chosen), or ‘the king of emptiness’. bde chen ming is a nominal clause, ‘[his] name [is] great bliss’. The refrain could also be one sentence with the king as agent: ‘the king, emptiness, named great bliss, destroyed the towns…’. Munidatta (cp.48.m4) says the towns are destroyed merely by hearing the name ‘great bliss’, which ties the two lines together without settling the grammar.
rgyal po is linked to raja, ‘king’, the glossary's general entry for a king; it was not among the detected hits.

lines.translit: /rnga sgra dung skad gzhom du med pa'i dbyangs rnams sgrogs/
lines.en: The sound of the [drum]{drum} and the call of the [conch]{conch} proclaimed the [unstruck]{anahata} melodies

flags.note: gzhom du med pa, ‘that cannot be destroyed, invincible’, is the regular Tibetan for anāhata; the glossary's ‘unstruck’ is used. In a battle song the sense ‘invincible’ is also live.
sgrogs is a present (or imperative) form; I render it as past to match the narrative and byas in 3b. skad is ‘voice, call, cry’; dbyangs ‘melody, tone’.

lines.translit: /gti mug srid pa'i dpung rnams ring du 'da' bar byas/
lines.gloss: delusion · of existence · armies · far off · made to pass
lines.en: and drove the [forces of existence]{bhavabala} and of [delusion]{moha} far off.

flags.note: gti mug srid pa'i dpung rnams: ‘the forces of delusion and of existence’ (as the glossary's army entry reads it) or ‘the forces of deluded existence’. I put existence first so that the glossary's ‘forces of existence’ stays whole. The agent of byas is not named: the English lets the drum and conch of 3a drive the forces off; it could be the army of 1b, or the yogin whom Munidatta tells to make the army of existence without intrinsic nature (cp.48.m5).
ring du 'da' bar byas is literally ‘made [them] pass far away’: drove off, routed. 'da' ba is also the verb of passing beyond, as in mya ngan las 'das, nirvāṇa.

lines.translit: /dkyil 'khor gsum gyi skyon rnams me yis bsreg par byas/
lines.gloss: maṇḍala · of three · faults · by fire · made to burn
lines.en: [Fire]{fire} burnt away the faults of the three [maṇḍala]{mandala}s

flags.note: me yis is instrumental, ‘by fire’, and no agent is named for 4a or 4b. I make fire the subject of both lines. Alternatives: the passive, ‘the faults of the three maṇḍalas were burnt by fire’, with 4b's agent left unexpressed; or an agent carried over from earlier lines (the army of 1b, the king of 2b). Munidatta (cp.48.m6) has the faults burnt with the fire of great bliss and the gathering done with the fire of the unfalling bodhicitta, without naming who acts.
dkyil 'khor is also ‘circle, district’; the line does not name the three maṇḍalas (Munidatta: ‘body and the rest’, cp.48.m6). skyon is ‘fault, flaw, defect’.

lines.translit: /bde ba'i grong khyer rtse mor gnas nas thams cad bsdus/
lines.gloss: of bliss · town, city · at the summit · having dwelt · all · gathered
lines.en: and, dwelling on the summit of the [town]{town} of [bliss]{sukha}, gathered everything in.

flags.note: bsdus, past of sdud pa, is ‘gathered, collected’, but also ‘withdrew, dissolved’ (the Tibetan word for yogic withdrawal, saṃhāra) and ‘brought under control’. I chose ‘gathered everything in’.

grong khyer normally means ‘city’ (Sanskrit nagara, pura), and a summit (rtse mo) suggests a citadel; the glossary's town covers grong khyer, so ‘town’ is used. The comment has ‘the summit of the wheel of great bliss’ (cp.48.m6) where the line has ‘the town of bliss’, and ‘great bliss’ where the line has ‘bliss’ (bde ba); I have not harmonized them.
gnas nas, ‘having dwelt, dwelling’, belongs to the unnamed agent of the line (here fire; see 4a).

lines.translit: /sor mo gyen du bslang nas kuk+ku rI pa smra/
lines.gloss: finger · upward · having raised · Kukkurīpa · says

flags.note: The line names the poet kuk+ku rI pa, without the honorific zhabs of the heading; the glossary's ‘Kukkurīpāda’ is used. ‘Kukkurīpa’ would be closer to this line.

The line does not explain the gesture. Munidatta's Sanskrit repeats it (aṅgulimūrdhīkṛtya, ‘having raised the finger’); the Tibetan comment has sor mo'i steng du byas pa, ‘made on top of the finger’ (cp.48.m1).

lines.translit: /'di ni 'jig rten gsum du bde ba chen pos rgyal/
lines.gloss: this (topic) · over the three worlds · by great bliss · conquers

flags.note: 'di ni stands before 'jig rten gsum, so it is a pronoun, ‘this’ (a Tibetan demonstrative qualifying the noun would follow it): ‘This conquers the three worlds by great bliss’, ‘this’ being perhaps what the raised finger points to. With rgyal, 'jig rten gsum du can mean ‘over the three worlds’ (chosen, as ‘conquers’) or ‘in the three worlds’. Munidatta's Sanskrit (cp.48.m1) cites etat trailokyam, ‘this threefold world’, and says that it, the fault of appearance of body, speech and mind, is conquered (jitaḥ) by great bliss: he takes the three worlds as what is conquered. Alternative: ‘These three worlds are conquered by great bliss.’

notes.text: Song 48 is missing from the Nepal palm-leaf manuscript that Shastri edited. Its heading, all ten lines and most of Munidatta's comment (cp.48.m2–cp.48.m6) survive only in the Tibetan translation of the commentary (Toh 2293), which quotes each song before commenting on it. This draft is therefore a translation of a translation: it renders the Tibetan, gives Wylie in the transliteration, and does not try to reconstruct the lost Old Bengali. Of Munidatta's Sanskrit only one passage survives, his comment on couplet 5 (cp.48.m1), printed by Shastri.

Munidatta, in the Tibetan, introduces the song by saying that Kukkurīpāda states the meaning of [reality]{tattva} (de kho na nyid) ‘with other words’ (sgra gzhan gyis), apparently in a different set of terms (cp.48.m2). As usual he leaves the refrain out of his count: after the refrain (cp.48.m4) he calls couplets 3, 4 and 5 his second, third and fourth verses (cp.48.m5, cp.48.m6, cp.48.m1).

The heading names the melody pa Da ha. The glossary files it under Paṭamañjarī, the rāga of song 1, as a shortened form: in other headings the Tibetan translation transcribes Paṭamañjarī as pa Ta ha many+dza ri or pa Da ha many+dza ri, or half-translates it as pa Ta ha'i snye ma, pa Da ha'i tshogs pa or rnga'i tshogs pa, ‘cluster of drums’, which shows its translators taking the first part of the name as paṭaha, a drum. Here only that first part is given. A distinct rāga named Paṭaha, or the drum paṭaha itself (Tibetan pa Ta ha, song 19), cannot be ruled out.
[Rāga]{raga}: a melodic mode of Indian music; each song is headed by the rāga to which it is sung. The Tibetan word is glu dbyangs, ‘melody’.

The [vajra]{vajra} is the thunderbolt-diamond, the emblem of the indestructible in tantric Buddhism; with the [lotus]{lotus} (Tibetan chu skyes, ‘water-born’) it forms the standard tantric pair of male and female. Here the pair enters the battlefront (g.yul ngo, ‘the face of battle’), and the whole song keeps to war: a mustered army, destroyed towns, war drums and conches, an enemy driven off, fire, and a summit occupied at the end.

Munidatta, in the Tibetan, says that Kukkurīpāda leads in the vajra and the lotus, ‘likewise means and wisdom’ (thabs dang shes rab), of the nature of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, in order to stop ‘the battlefront of the sound of objects’ (yul gyi sgra'i g.yul ngo; the phrase is obscure, and sgra may also mean ‘word’). He explains [sameness]{samata} as the joining in sameness (mnyam pa nyid du sbyor ba) of the essence of great bliss, one in nature, by the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, and quotes a scripture (lung): whoever sees the reality of one thing surely sees the reality of all things, for the nature of all things is the nature of one (cp.48.m3).

Munidatta's Tibetan gloss on sameness ends with a transcribed word: ‘that very joining is its dA ri kA’ (de nyid de'i dA ri kA'o). The glossary records dA ri ka as the Tibetan transcription of dārikā in song 28, where Munidatta glosses the courtesan (dārī) as Nairātmā (see [courtesan]{dari}). If the same word stands here, the joining in sameness would be called the lord of yogis' dārikā, his ‘girl’ or consort; but the word is left unexplained and the identification is uncertain (cp.48.m3).

Munidatta, in the Tibetan, says the refrain states the power (mthu) of great bliss: ‘destroyed’ means that these objects and senses of the [maṇḍala]{mandala} of existence are destroyed merely by hearing the words ‘great bliss’ (cp.48.m4). His gloss links the destruction of 2a to the name given in 2b.

Drums and conch trumpets were sounded in Indian warfare to signal and rouse troops, and conches also in ritual. The line has these struck and blown instruments proclaim ‘unstruck’ melodies (gzhom du med pa, also ‘indestructible’); in Indian yoga the unstruck sound is the inner sound heard without one thing striking another.

Munidatta, in the Tibetan, says his second verse makes the same point clear. ‘Unstruck melodies’ are the sound of the drum and the sound of the conch proclaimed at the battlefront; and since this is produced in the midst of emptiness, he tells the yogin (kye'i rnal 'byor pa, ‘O yogin’) to make the army of the battle of existence [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava} (cp.48.m5).

[Maṇḍala]{mandala}: a circle or disc; in the tantras the circular layout of a deity's palace and retinue, and by extension a bounded sphere of practice or of the body (Tibetan dkyil 'khor, also ‘circle, district’). The line does not name the three; Munidatta, in the Tibetan, calls them ‘body and the rest’ (lus la sogs pa) (cp.48.m6).

Munidatta, in the Tibetan, says his third verse praises ultimate [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}: the faults of the three maṇḍalas, body and the rest, are burnt by the fire of great bliss, and, dwelling at the summit of the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}, one gathers with the fire of the unfalling bodhicitta of great bliss. He quotes the [Rativajra]{tx-rativajra}: bodhicitta is not to be given up, since vajra and lotus seal it (rgyas 'dabs pas, perhaps for rgyas 'debs, ‘seal’; uncertain) (cp.48.m6). Where the line has ‘fire’ and ‘the town of bliss’, the comment has ‘the fire of great bliss’ and ‘the summit of the wheel of great bliss’; the translation keeps the line's words.

Munidatta's own Sanskrit survives for this couplet: Kukkurīpāda, having raised his finger (aṅgulimūrdhīkṛtya), says, ‘O yogin’: ‘this threefold world’ (etat trailokyam; Shastri prints trailokyām) means that the fault of appearance of [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta} (kāyavākcittasya ābhāsadoṣa) is conquered (jitaḥ) by great bliss. He adds [Saraha]{p-saraha}'s line ‘while staying at home, do not go to the forest’ (ghara acchante mā jāṅga vaṇa…) (cp.48.m1). He thus takes the three worlds as what is conquered, where the Tibetan line, as translated here, makes ‘this’ the conqueror.

The Tibetan of Munidatta's comment on this couplet opens with words the Sanskrit lacks, ‘with the fourth verse he states the nature of the fruit’ (rkang pa bzhi pas 'bras bu'i ngo bo gsungs te); the Sanskrit fragment may have lost its opening along with the song. The Tibetan renders aṅgulimūrdhīkṛtya as sor mo'i steng du byas pa, ‘made on top of the finger’, has great bliss victorious over (las rgyal) the fault of appearance of body, speech and mind, and gives Saraha's line as ‘while you have a house, do not go to the forest’ (cp.48.m1).
A raised finger. The line does not say what the gesture signals: emphasis, a challenge, a victor's sign, or a pointer to the ‘this’ of the next line.

questions: Heading: is ‘Paṭamañjarī’ acceptable for the Tibetan's pa Da ha, or should the heading print ‘Paḍaha’ (or ‘Paṭaha’) in source form, with the link to Paṭamañjarī in a note? A rāga Paṭaha, or the drum paṭaha, cannot be ruled out.

2a: the town entry forbids ‘sense objects’ in any verse line where the town is, but this line names the objects itself (yul, viṣaya). I wrote ‘objects’, linked to visaya. Should visaya take ‘objects’ as a variant, or should the town entry's ban not apply where the song itself names the objects?

2b: is raja (‘king’) the right link for rgyal po? Do you prefer ‘emptiness, the king’ (apposition) or ‘the king of emptiness’, and should the refrain be read as one sentence (‘the king, emptiness, named great bliss, destroyed the towns…’)?

4a–4b: the Tibetan names no agent. I made fire the subject of both lines. Would you rather have the passive (‘the faults of the three maṇḍalas were burnt by fire’) with the agent unexpressed, or an agent carried over from the army of 1b or the king of 2b?

4b: grong khyer normally means ‘city’, and the summit suggests a citadel. Should the line read ‘the city of bliss’ (as mahasukha-pura has ‘city of great bliss’) rather than the glossary's ‘town’? And is ‘gathered everything in’ right for bsdus, which can also mean ‘withdrew’ or ‘dissolved’?

5b: I read 'di ni as the pronoun ‘this’ (‘This conquers the three worlds by great bliss’); Munidatta's Sanskrit cites ‘this threefold world’ and has it conquered by great bliss. Keep the Tibetan line's reading, or prefer ‘These three worlds are conquered by great bliss’?
1b: is mela (‘union’) acceptable for sbyor ba, or would you prefer ‘the army joined in sameness’, unlinked? Is tshogs better taken as a verb (‘mustered’) or as a noun (‘host’)?
5a: the line has kuk+ku rI pa without zhabs. Should p-kukkuri take ‘Kukkurīpa’ as a variant for the songs that survive only in Tibetan?
The comment on couplet 1 ends with the transcribed word dA ri kA (cp.48.m3). Do you accept the tentative link to dārikā in song 28, or should the note simply call it unexplained?
Tense: the narrative verbs are Tibetan past forms (zhugs, bcom, byas, bsdus), so the draft narrates in the past, with the closing speech in the present. Would you prefer the present throughout?
